summary: Beckett, twenty-two when he arrived in Paris in 1928, grew close to Joyce and helped him by reading and finding material as Joyce's eyesight worsened. The following year he published his first piece of prose: the opening essay "Dante… Bruno. Vico.. Joyce" in a 1929 collection defending the serialized manuscript of Finnegans Wake.

Beckett published the monograph Proust in London in 1931. Reading habit as a device that numbs perception, and memory as something that cannot be summoned by will, the essay laid out in advance the problems of time and repetition that his later novels would take up.

Beckett's late television play …but the clouds… takes its title and closing lines directly from Yeats's poem "The Tower" (in the 1928 collection The Tower). It is a case of Beckett, by then writing in French and away from Ireland, pulling a line of Irish poetry into a piece of stagecraft.

Studies of postwar European fiction repeatedly place the two together for narrating unspecified guilt and unending procedure in a dry, report-like voice. However, no document specifying which of Kafka's works Beckett read, or when, is cited for this pairing.

In his Cornell lectures on literature, Nabokov made Madame Bovary the center of a semester, analyzing its scene transitions and contrapuntal construction sentence by sentence. The posthumously published Lectures on Literature (1980) is the longest surviving record of Flaubert as his benchmark for prose.

Lectures on Literature (1980) includes a lecture that follows Ulysses to reconstruct a single Dublin day with maps and timetables. Nabokov ranked the novel as the summit of twentieth-century prose while rejecting Finnegans Wake, taking Joyce in two separate parts.

In his Cornell lectures, Nabokov covered Swann's Way and analyzed how memory reconstructs events belatedly. This reading, preserved in Lectures on Literature (1980), is read alongside the recollective structure of Speak, Memory.

In his Cornell lectures on Russian literature, Nabokov placed Tolstoy first among Russian prose writers and made Anna Karenina the semester's central text. His lecture notes, which reconstruct characters' movements and the flow of time as diagrams, survive in Lectures on Russian Literature (1981).

In Lectures on Russian Literature (1981), Nabokov placed Chekhov at the very top of Russian prose and analyzed "The Lady with the Dog" as the standard for the short story. He described the technique of handling emotion through the arrangement of objects, rather than stating it outright, as Chekhov's method.

In Lectures on Russian Literature (1981), Nabokov dismissed Dostoevsky as a writer who relied on cheap suspense and sentiment. Placing the argument over sin and redemption at the center of the novel, versus placing sentence-level precision and devices that test the reader at the center, splits the lineage of Russian prose into two directions.

In the interview collection Strong Opinions (1973), Nabokov repeatedly named Robbe-Grillet as a contemporary French writer worth reading. The two are discussed together in accounts of late-twentieth-century fiction for the way each measures the surface of narration with precision while withholding a character's inner life.

Camus attached the appendix "Hope and the Absurd in the Work of Franz Kafka" to The Myth of Sisyphus, pinpointing where Kafka's fiction pushes the absurd to its limit and then leaps to hope. In the work of formalizing the absurd as a concept, Kafka is the precedent he treated at greatest length.

In The Myth of Sisyphus, Camus analyzed Kirilov in Demons as a case of absurd suicide, and in 1959 he adapted the entire novel into a three-part play. This reading, which went back to his youth, shows how his concept of rebellion passed through the argument staged in Russian fiction.

The Rebel (1951) devotes a chapter to Nietzsche, setting the nihilism left behind after the death of God as a gate that rebellion must pass through. Camus read Nietzsche as an inheritance while breaking from the twentieth-century violence that had been justified in his name.

Camus adapted Faulkner's Requiem for a Nun into a French-language play, published in 1956. This work, which deals with the time that remains after a crime has been committed, is set alongside that same year's The Fall, and is the most concrete record of how he read American fiction.

The two were close within the same circle of Paris intellectuals immediately after the Liberation, and the relationship ended over a dispute waged in the pages of Les Temps modernes after The Rebel appeared in 1951. Beauvoir recorded the circumstances of that break in La Force des choses (1963), and The Mandarins (1954) transposed the same-era circle into fiction.

In "An Explication of The Stranger" (1943), Sartre read Camus's short declarative sentences and his cutting of emotional commentary as a technique drawn from American fiction, Hemingway's prose in particular, and this reading has since become a standard item in accounts of Camus's style. However, no primary record of Camus naming Hemingway as his own model is cited here.

In The Theatre of the Absurd (1961), Martin Esslin took the term "absurd" from Camus's essay but split the two: Camus stated it within a well-made, traditional form, while Beckett presented it by breaking the form itself apart. Two answers to the same problem divide the lineage of postwar theater.

Between 1945 and 1949, the two each rendered totalitarianism and the individual under it as allegory. Orwell worked through fable and dystopia, Camus through a city sealed off by plague, treating the same problem. There is no record of direct contact or mutual reading between the two; this map places them together for comparison.

In Paris in 1922, Stein read Hemingway's early drafts and demanded he strip out adjectives and explanation. The phrase she passed on, "You are all a lost generation," became the epigraph of The Sun Also Rises (1926) and hardened into a generation's name, and their mentorship and eventual break survive in two differing versions, in The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas (1933) and A Moveable Feast (1964).

In his 1958 Paris Review interview, Hemingway listed his literary forebears and placed Flaubert near the front. His working discipline of rewriting the same paragraph until he found the one right word is explained within this lineage.

In his 1958 Paris Review interview, Hemingway included Tolstoy on his list of forebears and repeatedly cited him as the standard for prose that deals with war. His war novels are read as that standard rewritten and narrowed down to short sentences and a single person's field of view.

Hemingway contributed to a 1924 Conrad memorial section of the transatlantic review in Paris, writing that if it would bring Conrad back to life, he would grind Eliot — exalted by the literary world of the time — into powder. It is a piece in which he stated his own position, under Conrad's name: choosing a prose that drives the story through to the end over experimentation with the sentence.

The two knew each other through the Paris bookshop Shakespeare and Company in the 1920s. Sylvia Beach's memoir (1959) records how Hemingway worked out a way to get Ulysses, banned from import into the United States, across the border.

In "Lear, Tolstoy and the Fool" (1947), Orwell pushed back against Tolstoy's attack on Shakespeare, challenging the very attitude of judging literature by moral certainty. The two answer in opposite directions the question of whether art should be subordinated to doctrine.

Both writers made the Spanish Civil War the central event of their prose, but Hemingway wrote the death of an individual within the Republican side's own narrative, while Orwell moved toward denouncing the purges inside that same camp. Scholarship on Spanish Civil War literature treats For Whom the Bell Tolls and Homage to Catalonia together as opposing records of the same event.

Feminist criticism treats the argument of A Room of One's Own (1929) — which shifted women's writing from a question of talent to one of material conditions: money, a room, time — as a direct forerunner of The Second Sex (1949). However, exactly where and how Beauvoir cited Woolf is not specified for this pairing.

Both women signed the "Manifesto of the 343," published in Le Nouvel Observateur in April 1971. The document, in which the signatories publicly declared they had had abortions and demanded a change in the law, was an occasion where the postwar Paris literary circle stepped forward as parties to the issue, and Beauvoir wrote the text.

Celan carried on translating Russian, French, and English poetry into German throughout his life, and a few of Dickinson's poems are among them. Dickinson's syntax, broken by dashes, has been read alongside the truncated lines of Celan's late poetry.

As the epigraph to "And with the Book from Tarusa," collected in The No-One's Rose (1963), Celan set a line taken from Tsvetaeva's "Poem of the End": "all poets are Jews." In his work of building his own vocabulary while translating Russian poetry into German, Tsvetaeva was both something he quoted and a fixed point of reference.

German-language Celan scholarship repeatedly points out traces of Rilke in the diction and imagery of the early collection Poppy and Memory (1952). Celan later moved to shed that inheritance, and no Rilkean tone remains in his late poetry, narrowed down to coinages and silence.

Since the prose piece "Conversation in the Mountains" (1959) used the form of a fable to write a conversation between two Jews that keeps missing itself, German-language scholarship has treated Celan together with Kafka within the lineage of Jewish German-language writers from the Habsburg periphery. However, which edition of Kafka Celan read, and when, is not specified here.

These are two directions for transcribing Southern speech as it is spoken. Hurston dissolved the storytelling of a self-governing Black town into the whole of her narration, while O'Connor rendered the set phrases of white Protestant Southern speech precisely, then overturned them at the ending. There is no record of direct contact between the two; this map places them side by side on the axis of Southern vernacular.

These are two directions for making Black Southern vernacular into a literary language. Hurston carried the idiom of transcribed storytelling directly over into her narration, while Ellison abstracted the same vernacular into the formal principles of blues and sermon and built it into the structure of a novel. There is no record of direct exchange between the two.

Ellison repeatedly stated that reading "The Waste Land" while at Tuskegee was the moment that turned him from music toward literature, and he included Eliot on the list of chosen forebears in "The World and the Jug" (1963–64). The construction of Invisible Man, which layers quotation and fragmentary episode, is the result of passing through this reading.

In "The World and the Jug" (1963–64), Ellison rejected the lineage Irving Howe had assigned him, writing that if Richard Wright was a relative he could not choose, Hemingway was a forebear he had chosen for himself. This distinction, which defines a Black writer's literary descent by chosen technique rather than by race, has been quoted repeatedly ever since.

Ellison included Dostoevsky on the list of forebears in "The World and the Jug" (1963–64). The construction that opens and closes Invisible Man with an anonymous narrator, holed up underground and explaining his own condition, is read alongside Notes from Underground.

Ellison included Faulkner on the list of forebears in "The World and the Jug" (1963–64), and in the essays collected in Shadow and Act (1964) treated him as one of the few white writers who pushed Black characters past stereotype. In the lineage of American fiction dealing with the South and race, he placed Faulkner directly ahead of himself.

In several interviews, Baldwin repeatedly named Henry James as the model for his own prose. His long sentences, which pile up subordinate clauses before reversing direction at the end, and his setup of placing an American in Europe to observe, are devices that came from James.

Each, in his own essay, refuted the reading that imposes the duty of protest fiction on Black writers — Baldwin in "Everybody's Protest Novel" (1949), Ellison in "The World and the Jug" (1963–64). Scholarship on postwar African American literature reads these two essays together as one generation's answer to the same problem.

In a lecture collected in Mystery and Manners (1969), O'Connor wrote that no Southern writer can stand his mule and wagon on the track when the Dixie Limited comes roaring down — a sentence that named Faulkner as that train. Finding a way to write the same region without overlapping him was her formal problem.

In her theory of fiction in Mystery and Manners (1969), O'Connor quoted the goal Conrad had stated — by the power of the written word, to make the reader see — as her own goal. Her principle that one must begin by rendering the visible world accurately stands on this citation.

Scholarship on the twentieth-century American short story traces a lineage of endings that resolve through a shift in perception rather than in the plot, starting with Chekhov and continuing into American short fiction, and treats O'Connor as a Southern, theological variant of that lineage. However, where O'Connor said she had read Chekhov is not specified here.

Robbe-Grillet included an essay on Beckett in For a New Novel (1963), reading Waiting for Godot as an example of theater sustained by nothing but presence on stage, without psychology or narrative. It is a piece that identifies Beckett's work as having already shown what he himself was trying to do in the novel.

In For a New Novel (1963), Robbe-Grillet rejected readings that reduce Kafka to symbol and allegory, and took as the basis for his own theory of narration the fact that the corridors and stairs in The Castle are, above all, literally there. For him, Kafka was a precedent not for metaphor but for objective description.

Scholarship on the nouveau roman locates the starting point of this lineage in the idea Flaubert stated in an 1852 letter — a "book about nothing," a novel sustained by style rather than subject. Robbe-Grillet's program, which strips out character and plot and makes narration itself the content of the novel, is that idea taken to its extreme.

Grouped together on the same Éditions de Minuit list in the late 1950s and both called nouveau roman writers, the two nonetheless erased different things from their narration. Following the program of For a New Novel (1963), Robbe-Grillet stripped out psychology and affect and left only the measurement of objects, while Duras erased proper names and tense but left affect in place.

To the question of what to write with after the massacre, the two answered in opposite directions. Celan broke apart the perpetrators' language and reassembled it into poetry that resists reading, while Szymborska kept the surface of everyday speech and joking and dealt with the same century's violence through lists of numbers and objects. There is no record of direct exchange between the two.

These are two ways for poetry to record state violence. Akhmatova kept "Requiem," which could not be printed, in a voice of mourning and passed it on by memorization, while Szymborska carried the same problem over into the tone of statistics and lists of objects. There is no record of direct contact between the two; this map places them together for comparison.
